title: Growing crops
big_idea: Farmers raise the yield of a crop by giving plants what they need, removing what competes with or eats them, and breeding better varieties.
goals: I can explain how fertilisers, pesticides, greenhouses and machines increase crop yield, and how pests and population growth change the food supply.
I can describe how new varieties are made by cross-breeding and selective breeding, and interpret the results of a fertiliser investigation.

keywords.meaning: the amount of useful product a farmer gets from a crop
a substance added to soil that contains mineral salts to help plants grow
animal waste used as a natural fertiliser
a microorganism that breaks down dead material and waste
a substance that kills pests (organisms that damage crops)
a pesticide that kills fungi that cause plant diseases
a plant growing where it is not wanted, competing with the crop
a group of plants bred to have certain characteristics
breeding only from the plants with the wanted characteristics, generation after generation

misconceptions: Fertiliser is plant food. Fertilisers supply mineral salts (nitrates, phosphates, potassium); the plant still makes its own food by photosynthesis.
Herbicides and insecticides are different from pesticides. They are both types of pesticide: a pesticide is any substance that kills a pest.
More fertiliser always means more growth. The bean plant data show growth falling again with too much fertiliser; there is an optimum amount.
safety: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules.
equipment: Worksheets (standard and Chinese key words versions)
Mini whiteboards for the quick check (optional)
A packet of artificial fertiliser and a photo of manure spreading to pass round (optional)

slides.subtitle: How do farmers get the biggest harvest from the same field?
slides.notes: Lesson 5 of 9B. We move from the plant to the farm: what a farmer does to raise the yield, and the problems that come with it (next lesson).

slides.title: Do Now: more from the same field
slides.caption: Spreading fertiliser
prompt: 1. What does the yield of a crop mean?
2. Name three things a crop plant needs that a farmer can provide.
3. Suggest why a farmer might remove a hedge from the edge of a field.
slides.notes: Answers: the amount of useful product from the crop; e.g. water, mineral salts (fertiliser), light (greenhouse), warmth, protection from pests; to make space for big machines and more crop. Keep question 3 in mind for next lesson: hedges are habitats.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point to the key words box on the worksheet; three of today's words end in -cide, which means 'kills'.

slides.title: 35 per cent more food
slides.caption: Spraying a crop
slides.question: Farms in the UK today produce 35% more food from each square metre of land than they did in 1973. How?
text: Talk to a partner. Make a list of everything a farmer could change.
slides.notes: Build a list on the board: fertilisers, pesticides, better varieties, machines, greenhouses, irrigation, removing hedges. The Challenge question asks students to explain three of these, so leave the list up.

slides.title: Fertilisers and the best conditions
slides.caption: Manure from farm animals is a natural fertiliser
text: Fertilisers contain mineral salts that help plants grow: nitrates, phosphates and potassium.
Artificial fertilisers are cheap, dissolve in water and act fast.
Manure (animal waste) is natural: decomposers break it down and release the mineral salts slowly.
Greenhouses protect crops from changes in abiotic factors such as temperature, wind and rain.
Machines plant and harvest faster than people; forests and hedges are cleared to make room for them.
slides.key_idea: Fertiliser supplies the mineral salts a plant builds with; the plant still makes its own food.
slides.notes: Ask: too little phosphate gives poor root growth; what does too little nitrate give? Poor growth and yellow leaves (proteins and chlorophyll). Manure is spread before planting so the decomposers have time; artificial fertiliser is sprayed on the growing crop because it works at once.

slides.title: A fertiliser investigation

chart.title: Mean increase in height of bean seedlings after one week
chart.x_title: Liquid fertiliser added to each pot

text: Four groups each grew 20 bean plants in identical pots, one plant per pot.
Each group added a different number of drops of the same liquid fertiliser.
Describe the trend from 2 to 6 drops.
What happened with 8 drops?
slides.key_idea: More fertiliser helps up to a point; too much can harm the plants. There is an optimum amount.
slides.notes: Trend: growth increases as fertiliser increases from 2 to 6 drops; at 8 drops growth is lower. Why might too much fertiliser harm a plant? Too concentrated a solution around the roots can stop them absorbing water (link to osmosis in 9C). Students plot this chart on the worksheet.

slides.title: Pesticides
slides.caption: Aphids suck sugary sap from the phloem
text: Pests are organisms that damage crops. Pesticides kill them.
Insecticides kill insect pests such as aphids.
Fungicides kill fungi that cause plant diseases such as rust.
Herbicides (weedkillers) kill weeds, which compete with the crop for water, light and mineral salts.
Selective herbicides kill broad-leaved weeds but not narrow-leaved crops such as wheat.
slides.key_idea: -cide means 'kills': insecticide, fungicide and herbicide are all pesticides.
slides.notes: Why does killing aphids raise the yield? Aphids take the sugar solution from the phloem, so less sugar reaches the grain or fruit. Selective herbicides are expensive: farmers in low-income countries may weed by hand instead (Stretch 2).

slides.title: New varieties
slides.text: A variety is a group of plants bred to have certain characteristics, such as resistance to rust disease or short stems that do not blow over.
slides.key_idea: Cross-breeding: two varieties bred together to combine their characteristics. Selective breeding: only the best plants are used to breed, generation after generation.
slides.notes: Walk through the diagram: choose the shortest plants, breed them, choose the shortest of their offspring, repeat. Modern wheat is short and rust-resistant; a 1950s variety is tall and gets rust, so it is no longer grown. Challenge 1 uses the same idea with apples.

slides.title: Food supply and wild plants
slides.caption: IUCN Red List categories
text: In low-income countries many families grow their own crops. More people in the family, or more pests, means less food for each person.
Selective herbicides cost money, so some farmers weed by hand.
Farming can also destroy the habitats of wild plants. Endemic species, found nowhere else, are most at risk.
The IUCN Red List classifies species from least concern to critically endangered.
Before land is farmed, a plant ecologist may carry out an ecological audit.
slides.key_idea: Raising the food supply and protecting wild plants both matter; an ecological audit helps decide where farming can expand.
slides.notes: An ecological audit records which species are present, how many there are, where they are and which are endangered; the evidence goes into a report that can recommend Key Biodiversity Area status. The My thinking question asks what the audit should record.

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: Which type of pesticide kills weeds?
Name two mineral salts found in fertilisers.
Which fertiliser works more slowly, manure or artificial fertiliser? Why?
In the bean investigation, which number of drops gave the most growth?
slides.notes: Answers: herbicide; nitrates, phosphates, potassium (any two); manure, because decomposers must break it down first; 6 drops; a group of plants bred to have certain characteristics.

slides.title: Your turn
steps: Core: match the pesticides, plot the bean plant results on the grid and describe the trend, then fill the gaps on fertilisers.
Stretch: aphids and yield; selective herbicides; improving the investigation.
Challenge: breeding a yellow sweet apple; 35% more food since 1973.
Finished? Answer the My thinking question about the ecological audit.
slides.footer: Bar chart: the four groups are separate categories, so leave gaps between the bars. Label both axes with units.
slides.notes: Check the charts: category axis labelled with the number of drops, height axis in cm, bars with gaps. The common error is joining the tops of the bars with a line as if it were continuous data.

slides.title: Advice for the farmer
slides.prompt: Group 4 added 8 drops and got less growth than group 3 with 6 drops. What would you advise a farmer about how much fertiliser to use? What would you change in the investigation to be more sure?
frames: I would advise the farmer to ___ because ___.
To be more sure, I would ___ because ___.
One thing we do not know is ___.
slides.notes: Expected: use a medium amount (about 6 drops' worth), because more fertiliser reduced growth and costs money; repeat with more plants or more groups, test amounts between 6 and 8 drops, and measure for longer than a week. Also: we do not know the yield (beans), only the height.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: What do fertilisers contain that helps plants grow?
What do herbicides kill, and why does this help the crop?
Describe one step in selective breeding.
slides.notes: Answers: mineral salts such as nitrates, phosphates and potassium; weeds, which compete with the crop for water, light and mineral salts; choose only the plants with the wanted characteristic to breed from (and repeat over many generations). Collect the strips.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Farming problems: fertiliser in rivers, persistent pesticides, single varieties and the carbon cycle.
points: Yield is raised by fertilisers (mineral salts), greenhouses, machines and clearing land.
Too much fertiliser can reduce growth: there is an optimum amount.
Pesticides kill pests: insecticides, fungicides and herbicides; selective herbicides spare narrow-leaved crops.
New varieties come from cross-breeding and selective breeding over many generations.
Farming must be balanced against protecting wild plants, especially endemic species.
slides.notes: Homework: Workbook pages 20 to 22. Page 22 is the ecological audit report template; it can be done in pairs.

core.q: Match each type of pesticide to what it kills. Draw a line.

right: weeds with broad leaves, but not narrow-leaved crops such as wheat
all weeds (plants competing with the crop)
fungi that cause plant diseases such as rust

core.q: Students investigated fertiliser. Each group grew 20 bean plants in identical pots, one plant per pot, and added a different number of drops of the same liquid fertiliser. After a week they calculated the mean increase in height.

parts.text: Plot the results as a bar chart on the grid. Label both axes.
Describe the trend in the results between groups 1, 2 and 3.
What advice would you give a farmer about how much fertiliser to use, based on the result for group 4? Give a reason.

core.q: Complete the sentences. Use the word bank.
gap_lines: Fertilisers contain ____________ ____________ that help plants grow. Farmers use cheap ____________ fertilisers and natural ones such as ____________ (animal waste).
Microorganisms called ____________ break down manure and release the mineral salts, but this takes a long time.

stretch.q: Aphids are insect pests. They suck the sugary liquid (sap) from the phloem of plants. Explain how spraying a crop to kill aphids could increase the crop yield.
Selective herbicides kill weeds with broad leaves but not crops with narrow leaves.

parts.text: Suggest why a wheat farmer might want to use a selective herbicide.
Suggest why farmers in low-income countries may not use selective herbicides, and what they might do instead.

stretch.q: Describe one change you would make to the method of the fertiliser investigation to be more sure of the results. Give a reason for your answer.

challenge.q: An apple breeder has a yellow apple variety that is not sweet and a red apple variety that is sweet. Describe how the breeder could produce a new yellow, sweet variety. Use the words cross-breeding, select and generations.
Farms in the UK today produce 35% more food per square metre than they did in 1973. Explain three different ways farmers have achieved this.

worksheet.my_thinking: Before a farm is allowed to expand into a wild area, a plant ecologist carries out an ecological audit. Suggest three pieces of information the ecologist should record, and explain why each one matters.
exit: What do fertilisers contain that helps plants grow?
What do herbicides kill, and why does this help the crop?
Describe one step in selective breeding.

core: insecticide: insect pests such as aphids; fungicide: fungi that cause plant diseases; herbicide: all weeds; selective herbicide: broad-leaved weeds but not narrow-leaved crops.

a) Bar chart with gaps between bars, x-axis 'Drops of liquid fertiliser' (2, 4, 6, 8), y-axis 'Mean increase in height (cm)' with a sensible scale to 8 cm. b) As the amount of fertiliser increases from 2 to 6 drops, the mean increase in height gets bigger (more mineral salts, more growth). c) Use about 6 drops' worth, not more: with 8 drops growth was lower, so extra fertiliser is wasted money and can harm the plants.
stretch: Secure answer: aphids remove sugar solution from the phloem, so less sugar reaches the parts of the plant that are harvested (grain, fruit) and the plant has less glucose for respiration and growth. Killing the aphids leaves more sugar in the plant, so it grows more and the yield is bigger. Aphids can also spread plant diseases.

a) Wheat has narrow leaves, so a selective herbicide kills the broad-leaved weeds competing for water, light and mineral salts without harming the wheat, giving a bigger yield. b) Selective herbicides are expensive and need a sprayer; families growing their own food may not afford them, so they pull weeds by hand or hoe between the rows.

Secure answer: e.g. repeat the whole investigation (or use more plants per group) and calculate a mean, so that one unusual plant has less effect; or test more amounts between 6 and 8 drops to find the best amount; or run the test for longer than a week and measure the yield of beans, not just the height, because height is not the same as yield.
challenge: Secure answer: cross-breed the yellow variety with the red sweet variety so the offspring have a mixture of characteristics. Grow the offspring and select only the plants whose apples are yellow and sweet. Breed those together and again select the yellowest, sweetest from their offspring. Repeat over many generations until all the plants in the group produce yellow, sweet apples: a new variety.

Secure answer, any three: artificial fertilisers supply nitrates, phosphates and potassium so plants grow faster and bigger; pesticides (insecticides, fungicides, herbicides) stop pests, diseases and weeds reducing the yield; new varieties from selective breeding and cross-breeding give more grain per plant and resist disease; machines and larger fields (hedges removed) allow faster planting and harvesting; greenhouses and irrigation control abiotic factors.
exit: Weeds; weeds compete with the crop for water, light and mineral salts, so killing them leaves more for the crop and the yield rises.
Choose only the plants with the wanted characteristic (e.g. the shortest wheat) and breed from them; repeat with their offspring over many generations.
answers.my_thinking: e.g. which plant species are present (to find rare or endemic species); how many of each there are and where they grow (abundance and distribution, so the most important areas are known); whether any are on the IUCN Red List (to judge the risk of extinction); what the habitat is like and what else depends on the plants. Accept other sensible evidence.
